subject: Government
title: Nationalism and the Road to Independence
outline: Meaning and phases of Nigerian nationalism
The role of the press and trade unions
Constitutional conferences and the transfer of power

modules.title: Growth of Nigerian Nationalism
modules.html:
1. Meaning and Phases

Nationalism is the desire and struggle of a people for self-determination and freedom from foreign rule. Nigerian nationalism passed through three broad phases: an early elitist phase (1900–1922) of petitions by Lagos lawyers and merchants; a constitutional phase (1923–1944) of parties and press agitation for representation; and a mass phase (1944–1960) of nationwide parties, strikes and demands for full independence.

2. Factors that Promoted Nationalism

  1. Western education — produced a class exposed to ideas of liberty, self-determination and democracy.
  2. The Second World War (1939–45) — Nigerian ex-servicemen who fought in Burma and India saw whites defeated and returned questioning colonial superiority.
  3. The Atlantic Charter (1941) — Roosevelt and Churchill affirmed the right of all peoples to choose their government.
  4. The United Nations Charter (1945) — endorsed self-determination and trusteeship.
  5. Pan-Africanism — the Manchester Congress of 1945 (Nkrumah, Kenyatta, Du Bois, Padmore) and the ideas of Marcus Garvey.
  6. Independence of India and Pakistan (1947) and later Ghana (1957) — proved decolonisation possible.
  7. Racial discrimination in the colonial service, salaries and social life.
  8. Economic exploitation — marketing boards, expatriate control of trade, and the 1945 general strike over wages.
  9. Improved communications — railways, roads, telegraph and newspapers created a national arena.
  10. The nationalist press — the most effective mobilising instrument.

examples.q: Explain the significance of the 1945 general strike.
examples.a: Led by Michael Imoudu of the Railway Workers Union and supported by the press, the strike of 17 days (some 200,000 workers) was the first mass, cross-ethnic confrontation with the colonial state over cost-of-living allowances. It demonstrated that ordinary workers, not only the Lagos elite, could paralyse the colonial economy, deepened the alliance between unions and nationalists, and provoked the banning of Azikiwe's newspapers — which further radicalised opinion.

examples.q: How did the Second World War accelerate decolonisation in Nigeria?
examples.a: Nigerian troops of the Royal West African Frontier Force served in East Africa and Burma, saw European powers defeated by an Asian army and returned with new self-confidence and organisational skill. Britain emerged economically weakened and dependent on American and UN opinion, both hostile to empire, while the Atlantic Charter's promise of self-determination gave nationalists a moral weapon that colonial officials could not easily answer.

modules.title: The Press, Trade Unions and the Transfer of Power
modules.html:
1. The Nationalist Press

NewspaperYearFounder
Iwe Irohin1859Rev. Henry Townsend (first Nigerian newspaper)
Lagos Weekly Record1891John Payne Jackson
Lagos Daily News1925Herbert Macaulay
West African Pilot1937Nnamdi Azikiwe
Nigerian Tribune1949Obafemi Awolowo

The press exposed colonial abuses, articulated demands, unified opinion across regions and trained political leaders. Colonial responses included sedition laws, the Newspaper Ordinance and prosecution of editors.

2. Trade Unions

Michael Imoudu, 'Labour Leader Number One', and the Nigerian Union of Railwaymen mobilised workers; the 1945 general strike and later actions linked economic grievance to political demand. Unions supplied organisation, funds and mass membership to nationalist parties.

3. Steps to Independence

  1. 1951 Macpherson Constitution: ministers and regional legislatures.
  2. 1953 Enahoro self-government motion; London Conference.
  3. 1954 Lyttelton federal constitution.
  4. 1957 Internal self-government for East and West; Balewa becomes Prime Minister of the federation; Willink Commission on minorities.
  5. 1958 London Conference fixes independence for 1960; Willink reports, recommending a bill of rights instead of new states.
  6. 1959 Northern self-government; federal elections in December — NPC 134, NCNC 89, AG 73 seats, leading to an NPC/NCNC coalition.
  7. 1 October 1960 Independence, with Balewa as Prime Minister and Azikiwe as Governor-General.
  8. 1963 Republic declared.

4. Problems of the Nationalists

  • Ethnic and regional rivalry among parties and leaders.
  • Colonial repression: sedition laws, detentions, bans.
  • Illiteracy and rural apathy.
  • Shortage of funds.
  • Different pace of political development between North and South.
  • Divide-and-rule tactics and the co-option of traditional rulers.

examples.q: Assess the contribution of Herbert Macaulay to Nigerian nationalism.
examples.a: Called the father of Nigerian nationalism, Macaulay founded the NNDP in 1923, the first Nigerian political party, and won the Lagos elective seats repeatedly. Through the Lagos Daily News he campaigned against land seizure and the water-rate, defended the deposed Eleko of Lagos, and popularised constitutional agitation. In 1944 he became first president of the NCNC, giving the new mass movement legitimacy and linking the early elite phase to Azikiwe's nationwide phase.

examples.q: Why did the 1959 federal election produce a coalition government?
examples.a: No party won an overall majority in the 312-seat House: the NPC took about 134 seats, the NCNC 89 and the AG 73, because each party's strength was concentrated in its home region. Government formation therefore required agreement between two of them; the NPC and NCNC formed a coalition with Balewa as Prime Minister and Azikiwe as Governor-General, leaving the AG as opposition — a regional arithmetic that shaped and destabilised the First Republic.

quiz.q: The father of Nigerian nationalism is:
quiz.solution: Macaulay pioneered organised nationalist politics from 1923.

quiz.q: The West African Pilot was established in:
quiz.solution: Azikiwe founded the Pilot in 1937 to campaign for African rights.
Iwe Irohin was published in Abeokuta from 1859 by Rev. Henry Townsend.

quiz.q: The 1945 general strike was led by:
quiz.solution: Imoudu, leader of the railway workers, headed the strike.

quiz.q: The Atlantic Charter was signed in:
quiz.solution: Roosevelt and Churchill signed it in 1941, affirming self-determination.
The National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons was formed in 1944.

quiz.q: The Action Group grew out of:
quiz.solution: Awolowo transformed the Yoruba cultural society into a political party in 1951.
The Northern Elements Progressive Union was a radical Northern party led by Aminu Kano.
It recommended a bill of rights rather than the creation of more regions.

quiz.q: The 1958 London Conference fixed independence for:
Which party won the largest number of seats in the 1959 federal election?
quiz.solution: The NPC won about 134 seats and formed a coalition with the NCNC.

quiz.q: The Manchester Pan-African Congress held in:
quiz.solution: The fifth Pan-African Congress of 1945 demanded African independence.

quiz.q: Ghana's independence in 1957 influenced Nigeria by:
quiz.solution: Ghana's success under Nkrumah encouraged Nigerian nationalists.

quiz.q: Colonial governments countered the press with:
quiz.solution: Editors were prosecuted and papers banned under sedition provisions.

quiz.q: A major internal problem of Nigerian nationalists was:
quiz.solution: Regional parties competed rather than presenting a united front.

quiz.q: Nigerian ex-servicemen contributed to nationalism because they:
quiz.solution: Wartime experience abroad undermined the myth of European invincibility.
